modules.description: Learn the manual alphabet, basic introductions, polite manners, and conversational etiquette in NIOS Indian Sign Language.

lessons.lesson_title: Lesson 1: Introduction to NIOS ISL & Signing Space
lessons.theory: Indian Sign Language (ISL) is a full visual-spatial language with its own grammar, syntax, and morphology, completely separate from spoken English or Hindi. This lesson introduces the 3D signing space (extending from the top of the head to the waist and shoulder-to-shoulder). Standard signs must be made within this box for clear visual reception.
practical_instructions: Position yourself in front of a mirror or camera with back straight and relaxed shoulders.
Identify your signing space boundary by framing a box from your waist to the top of your head.
Practice centering your hands in the mid-torso area and maintaining direct eye contact rather than looking down at your fingers.

lessons.lesson_title: Lesson 2: Manual Alphabet - Two-Handed Letters (A to M)
lessons.theory: Fingerspelling in ISL is primarily a two-handed manual system. Your dominant hand acts as the 'active' hand (moving, pointing, tracing), while your non-dominant hand behaves as the 'base' hand (static platform). This lesson covers shapes and transitions from A to M.
practical_instructions: Keep your base hand completely flat and stable at chest level.
Use your active dominant hand to touch or tap on the base hand to execute letters A, B, and C.
Practice fingerspelling short letter sequences (e.g., 'CAB', 'BAG') smoothly, focusing on uniform heights.

lessons.lesson_title: Lesson 3: Manual Alphabet - Two-Handed Letters (N to Z)
lessons.theory: Building on letters A-M, this lesson completes the manual alphabet from N to Z. Smooth transitions are achieved through finger joint relaxation and wrist stability. Avoid bounding your arm or moving the static base hand during changes.
practical_instructions: Warm up finger joints with brief opening and closing movements.
Trace and form letters N through Z sequentially, paying close attention to clean finger configurations.
Fingerspell common names like 'RAVI' and 'SITA', keeping the pacing and tempo completely steady.

lessons.theory: Manners are crucial in Deaf culture. Greetings and polite words like 'Please', 'Thank You', 'Welcome', and 'Namaste' are signed with distinct hand movements and soft, respectful facial expressions. A deadpan face while signing 'Thank You' is grammatically incorrect.
practical_instructions: For 'Namaste', join both palms at chest level and bow your head slightly.
For 'Please', place your dominant flat palm on your chest and move it in a circular motion.
Coordinate your hand shape with a gentle, polite smile to convey genuine respect.

lessons.theory: To initiate a conversation in ISL, users learn basic communicative phrases like 'Hello, how are you?', 'I am fine', and 'What is your name?'. Attracting attention respectfully (using a light shoulder tap or a small hand wave) is a core cultural etiquette taught in this video.
practical_instructions: Perform a clean flat-palm wave at shoulder height to say 'Hello'.
Practice the light, non-intrusive hand wave used to attract a Deaf person's attention.
Practice spelling out 'MY NAME [Name]' using manual alphabet finger movements.

lessons.theory: Modifiers are signed to express quality, scale, or intensity. Basic modifiers like 'Good', 'Bad', 'Big', and 'Small' require matching non-manual facial cues. For 'Big', the eyes are widened and cheeks puffed, whereas for 'Small', eyes are squinted and cheeks pinched.
practical_instructions: For 'Good', perform a crisp chest-height thumbs-up motion.
For 'Big', spread both hands wide apart in front of your chest while widening your eyes.
Drill 'Good' vs 'Bad' and 'Big' vs 'Small' transitions rapidly to build muscle memory.

modules.description: Master kinship terms (mother, father, grandparents) and describing relations using spatial zones.

lessons.theory: Nuclear family signs include 'Father', 'Mother', 'Brother', and 'Sister'. ISL utilizes gender-coded quadrants in the signing space: male signs are typically signed higher near the forehead/mustache region, while female signs reside lower near the chin/cheek or earlobe region.
practical_instructions: For 'Father', trace your dominant index finger horizontally across your upper lip (representing a mustache).
For 'Mother', touch your cheek or point to your nose/earlobe to mark the female quadrant.
Ensure your hand placements are precise to avoid confusing gender indicators.

lessons.theory: Extended family signs cover 'Grandfather', 'Grandmother', 'Uncle', and 'Aunt'. These are compound signs, combining the base quadrant gender sign with the modifier 'Old' (mimicking a physical beard or bent posture) to denote older generations.
practical_instructions: To sign 'Grandfather', first trace the male mustache zone, then bring your hand down from your chin mimicking a long beard.
Practice the compound transition smoothly without a long pause between the gender sign and the age modifier.
Sign 'Grandmother' by combining the female chin/cheek tap with the old beard/bent-posture sign.

lessons.theory: Pronouns ('I', 'You', 'He', 'She', 'We', 'They') are represented indexically in ISL through pointing (indexing). Directing your index finger towards yourself establishes 'I', pointing forward is 'You', and pointing to set lateral spots establishes third-party pronouns.
practical_instructions: Point your dominant index finger directly to your chest center to sign 'I'.
Point directly forward to an imaginary viewer to sign 'You'.
Point to your right or left lateral boundary to establish 'He' or 'She' in the 3D space.

lessons.theory: Plural pronouns like 'We' and 'They' expand on basic pointing. Instead of a single static point, plural reference involves moving your index finger in a horizontal sweep or circular arc to encompass multiple imaginary positions in the 3D space.
practical_instructions: To sign 'We', point to your right chest, sweep the index finger outward in a front-circle, and tap your left chest.
To sign 'They', point to a lateral space and sweep your finger in a smooth, continuous horizontal arc.
Keep the sweep flat and stable at chest level to ensure readability.

lessons.theory: Possessive pronouns ('My', 'Your', 'His', 'Her') use a flat handshape (open palm) instead of an index finger pointer. The open flat palm represents possession and respect, signed towards the chest for 'My' or pushed forward for 'Your'.
practical_instructions: Place your open flat dominant palm firmly on your chest to sign 'My' (मेरा).
Push your open flat palm forward with fingers pointing upward towards the viewer to sign 'Your' (आपका).
Maintain a stable hand shape and use a clean, controlled movement forward.

lessons.theory: Signing basic social connections like 'Friend', 'Neighbor', and 'Colleague' relies on interactive manual movements. For 'Friend', users clasp both hands together in a gentle shake, symbolizing mutual support and structural partnership.
practical_instructions: Clasp both hands together, interlocking fingers in front of your chest to sign 'Friend' (मित्र).
Drill transition sequences: 'MY' (flat palm) -> 'FRIEND' (clasped hands) -> 'GOOD' (thumbs up).

modules.module_name: Module 3: Material World & Things Around Us
modules.description: Identify common household objects, structural terms, and personal items in your immediate environment.

lessons.theory: Household objects like 'Chair', 'Table', and 'Bed' are signed by replicating their functional forms or spatial outlines. 'Chair' simulates sitting down with hooked fingers, while 'Table' draws a flat horizontal surface in the air.
practical_instructions: To sign 'Table', hold both flat hands parallel at chest level, then move them apart horizontally and down to draw the legs.
For 'Chair', hook your dominant index and middle fingers and tap them on top of the non-dominant index/middle fingers (representing legs on a seat).
Keep your shapes rigid and clean to outline the objects clearly.

lessons.theory: Structural elements like 'Door', 'Window', and 'Wall' utilize flat palms (B-handshapes) as boundaries. 'Door' simulates opening/closing hinges with swinging palms, and 'Window' slides palms vertically or horizontally to mimic glass panels.
practical_instructions: For 'Door', hold both flat palms parallel, then swing your dominant palm outward from the static non-dominant palm.
For 'Window', place both palms facing in, and move your dominant hand up and down to show sliding panels.
Perform these movements cleanly, without shifting your elbows excessively.

lessons.lesson_title: Lesson 19: Core Places & Local Neighborhood Places
lessons.theory: Local places like 'House', 'School', and 'Shop' are signed using physical roofs or actions. 'House' uses both flat palms pointing together at an angle to outline a physical roof structure, while 'School' taps hands in an educational request.
practical_instructions: For 'House' (घर), join both flat hands at the fingertips to form an inverted 'V' roof angle.
Keep the roof peak aligned with your nose midline.
Practice smooth transitions: 'MY' (flat palm) -> 'HOUSE' (roof shape) -> 'BIG' (hands apart).

lessons.theory: Time grammar in ISL operates on a physical, linear timeline. The space directly in front of your chest represents the 'Present', moving your hands backward behind your shoulder indicates the 'Past', and moving forward indicates 'Future'.

For 'Today' (present), hold both flat hands parallel at chest level and move them down slightly.
Practice transition shifts: 'Yesterday' (back thumb) -> 'Today' (present level).

lessons.theory: This lesson introduces ISL sentence structure. Unlike English (which uses SVO), ISL strictly follows a **Subject-Object-Verb (SOV)** syntax. For example, the sentence 'I see a dog' must be signed in the exact order: 'I' (Subject) -> 'DOG' (Object) -> 'SEE' (Verb).
practical_instructions: Construct the sentence 'My sister reads a book'.
Sign 'MY SISTER' (Subject) first, then 'BOOK' (Object), and end with 'READ' (Verb).
Ensure there are no extra pauses between signs so the sentence flows naturally.

lessons.theory: Interrogative sentences ('What', 'Why', 'Where', 'When') follow two strict grammatical rules: (1) The question word is always placed at the very end of the sentence (e.g. 'Your name what?'), and (2) You must furrow your eyebrows as a mandatory grammatical marker.
practical_instructions: Sign the question: 'Where is your house?'.
First sign 'YOUR' (flat palm), then 'HOUSE' (roof shape), and end with 'WHERE' (question pointer).
Make sure to furrow your eyebrows while signing 'WHERE' at the end of the sentence.

lessons.theory: Negative sentences ('No', 'Not', 'Don't know') require terminal placement of the negative sign. A negative statement is accompanied by a headshake. This headshake is a linguistic marker, not just a physical gesture; signing 'NO' with a deadpan face is incorrect.
practical_instructions: Sign the sentence: 'I do not understand'.
Sign 'I' (Point chest), then 'UNDERSTAND' (flick forehead), and end with 'NOT/NO' accompanied by a headshake.
Ensure the headshake perfectly overlaps with the terminal negative sign.
